selected.name: Freshness over stockness
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the premise and wording take an uncommon route and avoid familiar joke templates; score 0 when the line is canned banter, a predictable invitation, or a stock pun.
selected.rationale: R22, R34, R42, and R44 use highly reusable conversational formulas, suggesting a property that can distinguish surface plausibility from originality.
member_names: Convincing pastiche of a real-world text genre
Naturalistic, distinct character voice in the dialogue
Originality versus a recognizable stock joke template
Standalone quotability without needing the unseen image

selected.name: Exact wordplay fit
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a homophone, near-homophone, spelling shift, or lexical substitution is precise and semantically apt; score 0 when there is no wordplay or the resemblance feels strained.
selected.rationale: R47, R50, and R60 rely on compact sound or spelling transformations, whereas several card-favored lines use looser associations.

selected.name: Meaningful numerical specificity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an exact number, count, or measurement makes the premise vivid and intensifies the joke; score 0 when numerical detail is absent, arbitrary, or irrelevant.
selected.rationale: The quantities in R26, R27, and R55 create distinctive comic premises rather than generic situations.
member_names: Oddly specific number or proper noun carries the joke

selected.name: Throat-clearing before the joke
selected.instruction: Score the amount of conversational preamble that precedes any comic content. 0 = the caption opens with discourse filler -- 'i don't know about you, but', 'believe it or not', 'on the plus side', 'enough about me', 'of course,', 'actually', 'i don't know.' -- that adds naturalness but no joke. 5 = a short functional lead-in that also sets up the payoff. 10 = the caption starts inside the joke with no runway at all. Score only the opening; a caption may be long and still open cold.
selected.rationale: Nearly every heavily card-favored item opens with filler: R29 ('i don't know about you, but'), R58 ('believe it or not'), R57 ('on the plus side'), R45 ('enough about me'), R27 ('actually'), R54 ('i don't know.') run card .752-.938 against dense .036-.338. The dense-high items open cold: R19, R38 ('i will give you no quarter'), R34. Filler is precisely what makes a line read as authentic natural speech, so any naturalness or voice criterion will pay for it while the dense model charges for the wasted runway.
member_names: Payoff density: no word that is not carrying the joke
Punchline economy with no throat-clearing setup

selected.name: Compactness with payload
selected.instruction: Score 10 when every word advances the setup, reinterpretation, or punchline and nothing feels expendable; score 0 when padding, repetition, or excess wording weakens the joke.
selected.rationale: The terse, forceful constructions in R09 and R46 contrast with the more generic conversational phrasing in R22 and R44.

selected.name: Clash between elevated/formal diction and mundane scene
selected.instruction: Score the degree of register mismatch between the caption's vocabulary and the ordinary or absurd situation it describes. 10 = formal, archaic, legalistic, or technical diction is applied to a mundane/absurd scene for comic contrast; 0 = the diction is uniformly casual/plain throughout, matching the scene register.
selected.rationale: R34/R51 use the archaic military phrase 'no quarter', R56 uses the Victorian-Holmesian 'cross word between us', and R26 uses legalistic phrasing ('implies consent') - all dense_high_card_low - producing a register clash the scorecard appears to undervalue relative to more register-flat dense_low_card_high lines.
member_names: Clash between elevated/formal diction and mundane scene
Institutional register deadpan over an absurd premise

selected.name: Distinctive speaker voice
selected.instruction: Score 10 when diction reveals a particular speaker’s attitude, role, or personality and would not sound interchangeable; score 0 when the voice is generic and characterless.
selected.rationale: R06’s faux-Watson diction, R17’s managerial euphemism, and R24’s evaluative pet-command voice show strongly differentiated speakers.

selected.name: Directness on taboo or transgressive subject matter
selected.instruction: Score how directly the caption confronts dark, risque, or uncomfortable content rather than softening or avoiding it. 10 = the caption states taboo or edgy content plainly, with no cushioning; 0 = the content is entirely safe, warm, or family-friendly with no edge.
selected.rationale: R06 ('you should see the breasts') and R26 ('exposed skin implies consent') and R47 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') are all dense_high_card_low and confront blunt/dark material head-on, in contrast to gentler dense_low_card_high items like R12 ('try howling like a wolf, it's hysterical') or R60.
member_names: Directness on taboo or transgressive subject matter

selected.name: Sustained double meaning across the whole line
selected.instruction: Score whether the caption's key words operate on two simultaneous levels of meaning across the entire line, versus containing only one clever word embedded in an otherwise single-register sentence. 10 = the whole caption sustains a coherent double reading start to finish; 0 = purely literal, single-register meaning throughout.
selected.rationale: R33 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes') and R46 ('i love that it's 100 wool') both sustain a literal-sheep/idiomatic double reading across the full line and are dense_high_card_low, compared to single-register lines like R60 ('in that case, i'm gonna eat dessert first') which is dense_low_card_high.
member_names: Sustained double meaning across the whole line

selected.name: Idiomatic frame transformation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar idiom, title, proverb, or lyric is recognizable but altered into a fresh, situation-specific meaning; score 0 when no such frame exists or it is merely repeated.
selected.rationale: R06, R25, and R48 preserve recognizable phrases while redirecting them, a pattern underrepresented by more literal lines such as R34.

selected.name: Vivid scene specificity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the caption evokes a concrete, unusual scene with identifiable roles, objects, and actions; score 0 when it could be pasted into many unrelated scenes without change.
selected.rationale: R27 and R57 imply sharply particular situations, while R22 and R34 rely on broadly reusable restaurant or invitation language.

selected.name: No self-commentary on its own funniness
selected.instruction: Score whether the caption stays inside its situation or steps out to appraise the joke. 0 = the caption labels its own material as amusing, ironic, thematic, or notable ('it's hysterical', 'that must be exciting', 'is a really cool band name', 'i think there's a theme'), or otherwise tells the reader how to react. 5 = mild evaluative language that could plausibly be in-character. 10 = the speaker is entirely absorbed in the situation and never comments on the humor; the line would be said the same way if it were not funny.
selected.rationale: Four of the most card-favored items announce their own joke: R24 ('it's hysterical', card .888 / dense .142), R45 ('that must be exciting', card .730 / dense .065), R57 ('a really cool band name', card .924 / dense .021), R17 ('i think there's a theme', card .813 / dense .128). Nothing on the dense-high side does this -- R19, R43, and R59 simply state a fact and stop. A rubric with criteria about clarity of comic intent or signposting will actively credit the self-commentary that the dense model treats as a defect.
member_names: Label mode where the name itself is the joke
No self-commentary on its own funniness

selected.name: Coherent causal twist
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the punch follows from a surprising but inferable chain of implications; score 0 when it is only a topical association, arbitrary juxtaposition, or non sequitur.
selected.rationale: R31 and R39 connect their premises to loosely related punchlines, whereas R57 and R55 make their unexpected turns more causally legible.

selected.name: Late twist or escalation in the final clause
selected.instruction: Score whether the caption sets up an expectation early and then overturns or sharpens it in its closing words, producing a distinct turn. 10 = a clear rug-pull or sharpening twist lands specifically at the end of the line; 0 = the caption proceeds as one flat, predictable statement with no turn.
selected.rationale: R04 ('581 days without an accident, and then you show up') turns sharply on its final clause and R47 ('my mom lost 45 pounds and my dad lost a leg') turns on its second half - both dense_high_card_low - versus single-beat lines like R60 ('in that case, i'm gonna eat dessert first', dense_low_card_high) which build to no comparable late turn.
member_names: Late twist or escalation in the final clause

selected.name: Speaker asserts and acts, rather than asking and hedging
selected.instruction: Score the speaker's stance toward the person addressed. 10 = a confident declarative that does something in the scene -- issues a threat, delivers a verdict, refuses, insults, or reframes the other party's position -- so the line changes the situation. 5 = a neutral observation or a question that carries real edge. 0 = a hedged question, a request for reassurance, or an agreeable pleasantry that leaves everything as it was. Score stance and force, not politeness.
selected.rationale: The dense-high side is full of lines that act on the addressee: R38 ('i will give you no quarter'), R22 ('no. no quarter will be given'), R10 (a flat contradiction), R06 ('and then you show up'), R55 (a reframing) run dense .656-.994 at card .028-.372. The card-favored side asks and defers: R20 ('are you sure the boss is cool with this?'), R26 ('you're sure it's wild caught?'), R48 ('can i get a discount?'), R08 ('you seem really nice'), R45 all reach card .582-.781 on dense .028-.214. Well-formed polite dialogue reads as high-quality writing to a criterion bank while carrying no comic force.
member_names: Speaker asserts and acts, rather than asking and hedging

selected.name: Staccato repetition or fragmenting punctuation
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption uses repeated short clauses, sentence fragments, or unusual punctuation (ellipses, an isolated single word set off by a period, trailing dashes) purely for rhythmic emphasis. 0 = normal single-clause punctuation; 10 = heavy fragmenting/repetition for emphasis. Score only the presence of this typographic/rhythmic device, not whether the emphasis is effective.
selected.rationale: R25 'six feet dude. six. feet' (dense_pct=0.040, card_pct=0.962) fragments the same two words three times for emphasis, and R07 'the difference between let's eat, chefs! and let's eat chefs! is not as subtle as one would think.... --' (dense_pct=0.563, card_pct=0.017) uses trailing ellipsis-and-dash punctuation — both show unusual fragmenting/punctuation choices that are formal, not content-based.
member_names: Terseness / token economy of the caption as written

selected.name: Stock dialogue scaffolding
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only how much the caption uses familiar conversational setups, such as greetings, invitations, disclaimers, or routine dialogue openers; do not judge whether the setup works.
selected.rationale: Editing or coaching may encourage standardized conversational templates that affect textual reception; coaching can also sometimes improve genuine execution. Examples include R26, R35, R47, and R60.
member_names: Reliance on a stock idiom or catchphrase
Reliance on the single most obvious stock hook for the scene (MODE 2)

selected.name: Pandemic or geopolitical event-pinning vocabulary
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption references a specific, dateable real-world event or era outside party politics — such as vaccination status, a named ongoing war or invasion, or other period-specific current-events shorthand. 0 = no such reference; 10 = the caption's premise depends entirely on that event being current. Score only the presence of such era-pinning content, not whether the reference is used cleverly.
selected.rationale: R24 'of course, i'm vaccinated. do you think i'm crazy' (dense_pct=0.053, card_pct=0.582) and R39 'let's go. mommy doesn't have enough quarters to invade russia' (dense_pct=0.322, card_pct=0.898) both pin the joke to a specific era's news and both land in dense_low_card_high, a distinct cluster from the party-politics cases in B04.
selected.upstream_parent: submission timing pinned to a specific real-world event or era (pandemic, geopolitical conflict) rather than a timeless reading of the cartoon

selected.name: Phonetic wordplay compressed into a single word
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of sound-based wordplay in the caption: homophones, near-homophones, portmanteaus, respellings, or an idiom whose ordinary meaning is displaced by a same-sounding alternative. 0 = no sound play, all words used in their plain sense; 5 = a mild double sense that does not depend on pronunciation; 10 = the caption's whole content is a phonetic substitution or coinage. Score only the presence and density of sound play as an observable linguistic operation. Do NOT judge whether the pun works, is groan-worthy, is original, or is good.
selected.rationale: Pun-carrying items cluster hard in dense-high/card-low: R34 ('it's so ewe'), R39 ('wreckmaninoff'), R19 ('i suspect vowel play'), R44 ('could you pull the wool over my eyes'), R26 ('the gravity of our situation'), R60 ('88 keys and no locks'). A phonetic pun is a lexical mechanism, not a merit level -- puns range from superb to dire -- but it is nearly invisible to criteria written in propositional terms ('does the caption establish a situation', 'is there a reversal'), so its presence systematically depresses scorecard rank independently of quality. Declaring it a nuisance keeps 'contains a pun' out of the bank in both directions.
member_names: Phonetic wordplay compressed into a single word

selected.name: Off-colour, bodily and dark-subject content
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of transgressive content in the caption: sexual or anatomical reference, consent or harassment themes, bodily-function or scatological words, bodily harm, death, cannibalism, or cruelty toward a named party. 0 = wholly innocuous content; 5 = one mild edgy or bodily word; 10 = the caption's central content is sexual, scatological, violent or otherwise taboo. Score only the observable presence and intensity of such content. Do NOT judge whether the transgression is funny, gratuitous, offensive, well-handled, or good, and do NOT reward or penalise edginess; you are counting content type only.
selected.rationale: Transgressive content concentrates in the dense-high/card-low arm: R33 ('where we disagree is that exposed skin implies consent'), R48 ('you should see the breasts'), R40 ('we'll be pooped by the end of the night'), R17 ('my dad lost a leg'), with R06 and R09 carrying darker material on the other arm. Content category is orthogonal to how good the caption is as a contest entry -- taboo captions span the full merit range -- but explicit criteria almost always carry an implicit propriety filter, so this material is penalised or bonused as a class. Declaring it a nuisance prevents 'is it clean' and 'is it daring' from entering the bank under either sign.
upstream_parent_all_members: curation/engagement dynamics on the receiving side, where taboo or provocative content draws disproportionate attention or discussion independent of comic craft

selected.name: Quantification density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit numerals, counts, weights, durations, distances, or other measurements. Judge only quantity and salience; do not judge whether specificity is good.
selected.rationale: Numbers and measurements are conspicuous textual cues that may predict reception without being intrinsic evidence of quality. Examples include R14, R19, R24, R38, and R44.

selected.name: Identity-role markers
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit family, dating, occupational, religious, age, or other social-role labels. Judge only amount and specificity; do not judge whether the portrayal is good.
selected.rationale: Author identity may shape which roles appear in the text and may also influence genuine insight, making this a mixed nuisance. Examples include R14, R22, R49, and R51.

selected.name: Copyediting normalization
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of standardized punctuation, spacing, capitalization, apostrophe, and sentence-format conventions. Judge only visible editing conventions; do not judge whether the result is good.
selected.rationale: Professional editing can create recognizable textual polish and can also genuinely improve wording, so this is a sensitivity channel. Examples include R02, R11, R44, and R57.

selected.name: Cultural specificity
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, score only the extent of named people, brands, places, groups, media, or other culturally specific references; do not judge whether the references are apt or funny.
selected.rationale: An author's network or assumed audience may shape which recognizable references appear, independently of quality; the same cultural fluency may also enable genuinely stronger work. Examples include R20, R25, R30, and R31.

selected.name: Genre-pastiche of a non-cartoon written register
selected.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the caption mimics the fixed phrasing conventions of a specific, unrelated written genre — e.g. a restaurant review, a real-estate listing, or a dating-app message — rather than reading as spontaneous spoken dialogue. 0 = no genre mimicry; 10 = the caption reads as if lifted directly from that other genre. Score only the presence of the borrowed register, not whether the pastiche is executed well.
selected.rationale: R55 'love it -- perfect for a quick bite or an evening out' (dense_pct=0.268, card_pct=0.847) reads like restaurant-review copy, and R58 'if you're free after work, i know this hole-in-the-wall place you'll love' (dense_pct=0.170, card_pct=0.938) reads like a dating-app pitch — both genre-pastiche lines sit in dense_low_card_high.
member_names: Genre-pastiche of a non-cartoon written register
